opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there are a few big gaps. SWE-bench is a great benchmark: it's grounded in real GitHub issues from real repos, and the grading is based on actual tests passing. That's way better than toy puzzles. But it's still a pretty narrow slice of what a coding agent does day to day.

The first thing is that the tasks are very well-specified, at least in a sense. You get an issue, there's a hidden test that defines "correct," and the agent just has to make that test pass. In real use, the hardest part is often figuring out what the person actually wants. Users give you an underspecified request, and a good agent needs to ask a clarifying question, or make a reasonable assumption and flag it. SWE-bench doesn't reward any of that. If anything, it rewards just charging ahead.

Second, there's no notion of code quality beyond "the tests pass." Customers care a lot about whether the change is minimal, whether it matches the style of the codebase, and whether a human reviewer would actually merge it. You can pass a SWE-bench task with a pretty ugly hack, and that counts the same as a clean fix. In practice, if your agent produces hacky diffs, people stop trusting it fast.

Third, scope and the shape of the work. SWE-bench tasks are mostly bug fixes in Python repos, and they're mostly single-shot: one issue, one patch. Real work is much more varied. People build new features, do refactors across many files, write tests from scratch, debug flaky CI, or work in TypeScript or Go or some crusty internal framework. It's also often a long, interactive session where the person steers along the way. Collaborating over many turns is a different skill from autonomously solving one ticket.

And then there's the environment side. Real agents need to run commands, set up dependencies, deal with a broken dev environment, and know when *not* to do something destructive. Benchmarks mostly abstract that away.

So I'd say SWE-bench is a really useful signal for raw problem-solving ability, and improvements there have generally tracked real improvements. But once you're above a certain level, the things that make customers happy are judgment, communication, and taste, and those are much harder to put in a benchmark.

r002.rationale: It says agents should ask clarifying questions about underspecified requests, but does not state that clarification should happen before extended work begins.

r003.rationale: It says real work often involves long, interactive sessions where users steer along the way, and that benchmarks do not capture this skill.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think SWE-bench was incredibly useful for a specific moment. It gave us a clean, verifiable signal when nobody really knew if models could do real software engineering at all. But the place it diverges from what customers actually want is that SWE-bench is a closed-world problem. You get a fully specified issue, a repo that's already set up, a hidden test that tells you unambiguously whether you succeeded. The task is to write a patch. That's a very narrow slice of what engineers do all day.

When you watch people use Claude Code or Cursor or any of these tools, the hard part is usually not the patch. It's figuring out what the task even is. The ticket says "the export is slow" and you have to go understand which export, for which customers, what "slow" means to them, whether it's a database problem or a serialization problem, whether there's a reason it was built that way. There's no hidden test for that. Half the value of a good agent is asking the right clarifying question, or noticing that the thing you were asked to do is subtly wrong and saying so, and SWE-bench actively doesn't reward that. If the agent stops to ask a question, it gets a zero.

The second big gap is time horizon. SWE-bench tasks are mostly things a strong engineer does in twenty minutes to a couple hours. Customers increasingly want to hand off a day's worth of work, or a week's worth. And the failure modes at that scale are totally different. It's not "did you write the right three lines," it's "did you keep track of what you were doing, did you avoid breaking the thing you fixed yesterday, did you notice your test suite was green only because you accidentally skipped half of it." Those are agentic skills, planning and verification and recovering from your own mistakes, and a short benchmark just can't exercise them.

Third thing is the environment. SWE-bench is mostly popular Python open source repos. The models have seen Django and scikit-learn a thousand times in pretraining. A real customer has a 15 year old monorepo with an internal build system, flaky integration tests that take forty minutes, and conventions that only exist in some senior engineer's head. Generalizing to that is a very different problem than scoring well on repos that are, frankly, kind of in-distribution at this point. We've seen models that look great on the benchmark struggle with a weird Bazel setup or a codebase in a less common language.

And then there's the whole category of stuff that's about the output beyond the diff. Does the code look like something a human on that team would have written? Is the PR description useful? Did it leave the codebase in a state where someone can maintain it? SWE-bench grades on "tests pass," and you can pass tests with a truly horrible patch. Customers care enormously about the horrible patch because they're the ones who have to review it and live with it.

So I'd say the honest framing is that SWE-bench measures a necessary condition. If you can't do that, you definitely can't do the real job. But there's a widening gap between saturating it and actually being a good coworker, and the things in that gap, scoping, long-horizon reliability, taste, communication, are where I think most of the real progress is happening right now, and where we need better ways to measure it. Internally we lean a lot more on things like how often engineers actually merge what the agent produces without rewriting it, and how long people are willing to let it run unattended. Those are messier numbers, but they track what people are paying for.

r002.rationale: It says agents should ask clarifying questions when the task is unclear before attempting to solve the wrong problem; it also notes that SWE-bench penalizes stopping to ask.

r003.rationale: It describes user-facing clarification as valuable agent work that SWE-bench does not reward, identifying an interactive aspect current benchmarks miss.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention τ-bench or describe a customer-LLM and support-agent-LLM interaction.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest gap is that SWE-bench starts with a well-defined issue and a repository, and asks whether you can produce a patch that passes the tests. That’s useful, but it’s only part of what people need from a coding agent.

In real use, a lot of the work is figuring out what the task actually is. The user gives you an incomplete description, you have to find the relevant code, understand the constraints, and sometimes ask a question before making a change. And passing tests doesn’t necessarily tell you whether you built what the user wanted or whether the change is easy to maintain.

There’s also the interaction over time. A customer might ask for a change, look at it, and say, “Actually, let’s do it this other way.” The agent needs to handle that feedback well. So I’d view SWE-bench as a useful measure of a particular capability, but not a complete measure of how useful an agent is as a collaborator.

r001.rationale: The response discusses task discovery and constraints but does not identify access to outside information as a gap.

r002.rationale: It says that when a user gives an incomplete description, the agent may need to ask a question before making a change.

r003.rationale: It describes user feedback and changes of direction over time as part of real-world work, and says SWE-bench is not a complete measure of agent usefulness.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention τ-bench or describe its customer-and-support-agent interaction setup.

sol-6.1.text:
I think SWE-bench measures a useful but fairly narrow slice of the job. You start with an issue in an existing repository, and success is largely defined by whether your patch passes the tests. That’s a lot cleaner than what a customer usually hands you.

In real use, figuring out what to build is often part of the task. The request is ambiguous, the relevant context is spread across different places, and you might need to ask a question before you start coding. Then you need to run the application, check that the behavior actually makes sense, and produce something the person can review and maintain.

So there’s a gap between ‘can you solve this well-specified issue?’ and ‘can I delegate work to you?’ The benchmark is useful evidence for the first. Customers care about the second: how much work can they hand off, and how much supervision does it take to get a result they trust?
